egmo-2017-01.title: Two right-angle circles
egmo-2017-01.body:
We use directed angles $\measuredangle$ modulo $180^\circ$. Recall that if $Z$ is the centre of a circle through $X,Y,W$, then $\measuredangle XZY=2\measuredangle XWY$ (this is well defined modulo $180^\circ$).

**$N$ is the midpoint of $PS$.** The quadrilateral lies inside the angle $\angle DAB$, and so does segment $QR$. The line $QR$ leaves this convex angular region through its boundary on both sides of segment $QR$. It cannot leave through ray $AB$ on both sides (then it would be line $AB$). If it met ray $AB$ at $P$ on one side and never left the region on the other side, then $S$ would lie on the extension of $DA$ beyond $A$, outside the region, hence beyond $P$: the order would be $S,P,Q,R$ and $RS>PQ$, a contradiction. So $P$ and $S$ lie on opposite sides of segment $QR$, in the order $P,Q,R,S$, and $PQ=RS$ gives that $N$ is also the midpoint of $PS$.

**The angle at $N$.** Since $\angle PAS=90^\circ$, $N$ is the centre of the circle through $A,P,S$; since $\angle QCR=90^\circ$, $N$ is the centre of the circle through $C,Q,R$. As $P,Q,N$ are collinear,
$$\measuredangle ANC=\measuredangle ANP+\measuredangle QNC=2\measuredangle ASP+2\measuredangle QRC .$$
Now $\measuredangle ASP=\measuredangle DSR$ and $\measuredangle QRC=\measuredangle SRD$ (same lines), and in triangle $DSR$ we have $\measuredangle DSR+\measuredangle SRD=-\measuredangle RDS=\measuredangle SDR=\measuredangle ADC$. Hence
$$\measuredangle ANC=2\measuredangle ADC.$$

**The angle at $M$.** Since $\angle BAD=\angle BCD=90^\circ$, $M$ is the centre of the circle through $A,B,C,D$, so $\measuredangle AMC=2\measuredangle ADC$.

**Conclusion.** So $\measuredangle ANC=\measuredangle AMC$. The points $A,M,C$ are not collinear: otherwise $AC$ would be a diameter of circle $ABCD$, giving $\angle ABC=\angle CDA=90^\circ$, contradicting $\angle ABC>\angle CDA$. Hence $M,N,A,C$ lie on a circle (if $N=M$ there is nothing to prove). ∎

egmo-2017-02.title: Construction, then $f(3n)=3f(n)$
egmo-2017-02.body:
**$k=3$ works.** Colour $n$ by its residue modulo $3$ and let $f(n)=n$ if $3\nmid n$, $f(n)=2n$ if $3\mid n$. Then $f(1+2)=6\ne3=f(1)+f(2)$, so (ii) holds. For (i): if $m\equiv n\equiv0$, then $f(m+n)=2(m+n)=f(m)+f(n)$; if $m\equiv n\equiv1$ then $m+n\equiv2$, and if $m\equiv n\equiv2$ then $m+n\equiv1$, so in both cases $f(m+n)=m+n=f(m)+f(n)$.

**$k\le2$ is impossible.** (A colouring with one colour is a special case of two colours.) Take two colours and $f$ satisfying (i).
- With $m=n$: $f(2n)=2f(n)$ for all $n$.
- **Claim: $f(3n)=3f(n)$.** Let $c=f(n)$, $d=f(3n)$; then $f(2n)=2c$, $f(4n)=4c$, $f(6n)=2d$.
  - If $n,2n$ have the same colour: $d=f(n)+f(2n)=3c$.
  - If $n,3n$ have the same colour: $4c=f(n)+f(3n)=c+d$, so $d=3c$.
  - If $2n,4n$ have the same colour: $2d=f(2n)+f(4n)=6c$, so $d=3c$.
  - Otherwise $2n$ and $3n$ both have the colour opposite to $n$, and $4n$ has the colour opposite to $2n$, i.e. that of $n$. Then $f(5n)=f(n)+f(4n)=5c$ and $f(5n)=f(2n)+f(3n)=2c+d$, so $d=3c$.

If $f(x)=xf(1)$ for all $x$, then $f$ is additive, contradicting (ii). So let $a$ be the smallest positive integer with $f(a)\ne af(1)$. Then $a\ne1$, $a$ is not even (else $f(a)=2f(a/2)=af(1)$) and $a\ne3$ (as $f(3)=3f(1)$). So $a$ is odd and $a\ge5$, and $\frac{a-3}2,\frac{a-1}2,\frac{a+1}2,\frac{a+3}2$ are positive integers smaller than $a$.

Two of the three numbers $a,\frac{a-3}2,\frac{a+3}2$ have the same colour.
- $\frac{a-3}2,\frac{a+3}2$: $f(a)=\frac{a-3}2f(1)+\frac{a+3}2f(1)=af(1)$.
- $a,\frac{a-3}2$: $f(a)+\frac{a-3}2f(1)=f\!\left(\frac{3(a-1)}2\right)=3f\!\left(\frac{a-1}2\right)=\frac{3(a-1)}2f(1)$, so $f(a)=af(1)$.
- $a,\frac{a+3}2$: $f(a)+\frac{a+3}2f(1)=f\!\left(\frac{3(a+1)}2\right)=3f\!\left(\frac{a+1}2\right)=\frac{3(a+1)}2f(1)$, so $f(a)=af(1)$.

Each case contradicts the choice of $a$. Hence the smallest $k$ is $3$.

**Answer: $k=3$.**

egmo-2017-03.title: Chessboard colouring of the regions
egmo-2017-03.body:
**No.** In fact this holds even if Turbo chooses left or right arbitrarily at each intersection.

**A 2-colouring.** For each line choose one of its two sides as "positive". Colour a region of the plane white if it lies on the positive side of an even number of lines, black otherwise. Two regions sharing a segment of a line $\ell$ lie on the same side of every line except $\ell$, so they get different colours.

**Invariant.** While Turbo moves along a segment, there is a region on her left and a different-coloured region on her right. By symmetry of the colours, suppose that at the start the white region is on her left. We show this stays true at every turn. Suppose she arrives at the intersection $X$ of her line $\ell$ with a line $m$, moving "north" along $\ell$, with white on her left (west) and black on her right (east). Around $X$ the four regions alternate in colour: south-west white, south-east black, so north-east white and north-west black.
- If she turns right, she moves east along $m$; on her left (north) is the north-east region (white), on her right the south-east region (black).
- If she turns left, she moves west along $m$; on her left (south) is the south-west region (white), on her right the north-west region (black).

So she always has a white region on her left and a black region on her right.

**Conclusion.** A segment borders exactly two regions, one white and one black. Travelling along it in one direction puts the white region on the left, in the other direction the black region. By the invariant Turbo only ever uses the first direction. So no segment is traversed in both directions.

**Answer: No.**

egmo-2017-04.title: Induction with complements
egmo-2017-04.body:
In graph language: for every set $T=\{t_1<\dots<t_n\}$ of positive integers we must build a simple graph on $t_n+1$ vertices whose set of degrees is exactly $T$. We induct on $n$.

**Base $n=1$.** The complete graph on $t_1+1$ vertices: every degree is $t_1$.

**Step.** Let $n\ge2$ and assume the statement for all sets of $n-1$ positive integers. Consider
$$T'=\{t_n-t_{n-1},\ t_n-t_{n-2},\ \dots,\ t_n-t_1\},$$
a set of $n-1$ positive integers with largest element $t_n-t_1$. By hypothesis there is a graph $G'$ on $t_n-t_1+1$ vertices with degree set $T'$.

Add $t_1$ new isolated vertices to get a graph $G''$ on $t_n+1$ vertices; its degree set is $T'\cup\{0\}$. Let $G$ be the complement of $G''$ (two people play if and only if they are not joined in $G''$). Each vertex $v$ has $\deg_G v=t_n-\deg_{G''}v$. So the degree set of $G$ is
$$\{t_n-s: s\in T'\cup\{0\}\}=\{t_1,\dots,t_{n-1}\}\cup\{t_n\}=T.$$

This completes the induction: let the people play according to the edges of $G$. Every person has played some $t_i$ games, and every $t_i$ occurs. ∎

egmo-2017-05.title: Descent and insertion
egmo-2017-05.body:
Indices are cyclic modulo $n$. Each factor $a_i+a_{i+1}\ge2$ divides a power of $2$, so it is a power of $2$.

**(a) Odd $n$ work.** For odd $n\ge3$, the tuple $(1,1,\dots,1)$ gives the product $2^n=2^{2k-1}$ with $k=\frac{n+1}2$.

**Even $n$ do not.** *Lemma: if an expensive $n$-tuple exists with $n\ge4$, then an expensive $(n-2)$-tuple exists.* Let $a_t$ be a largest entry. Then
$$a_{t-1}+a_t\le2a_t<2(a_t+a_{t+1}),\qquad a_t+a_{t+1}\le2a_t<2(a_{t-1}+a_t).$$
Two powers of $2$, each less than twice the other, are equal: $a_{t-1}+a_t=a_t+a_{t+1}=2^r$, so $a_{t-1}=a_{t+1}$. Delete $a_t$ and $a_{t+1}$. In the new cyclic $(n-2)$-tuple, $a_{t-1}$ is followed by $a_{t+2}$, and $a_{t-1}+a_{t+2}=a_{t+1}+a_{t+2}$ was a factor before. So the new product equals the old one divided by $(a_{t-1}+a_t)(a_t+a_{t+1})=2^{2r}$, which is $2^{2(k-r)-1}$. It is a product of $n-2\ge2$ factors, each $\ge2$, so the exponent is at least $2$ and $k-r\ge2$ is a positive integer. The new tuple is expensive.

If an expensive $n$-tuple existed for some even $n$, applying the lemma repeatedly would give an expensive $2$-tuple: $(a_1+a_2)^2=2^{2k-1}$. That is impossible, since the left side is a square and an odd power of $2$ is not. **So the answer to (a) is: all odd $n\ge3$.**

**(b)** We prove by induction on $j\ge1$: every odd $m<2^j$ belongs to some expensive tuple.
- $j=1$: $m=1$ belongs to $(1,1,1)$.
- Step $j\to j+1$: let $m$ be odd with $2^j<m<2^{j+1}$, and put $r=2^{j+1}-m$. Then $r$ is odd and $r<2^j$, so by hypothesis $r$ occurs in an expensive tuple $(\dots,x,r,y,\dots)$. Replace this entry $r$ by the three entries $r,m,r$: $(\dots,x,r,m,r,y,\dots)$. The factors $x+r$ and $r+y$ are kept, and two new factors $r+m=m+r=2^{j+1}$ appear. The product is multiplied by $2^{2j+2}$, so it is still an odd power of $2$. The new tuple is expensive and contains $m$.

Every odd $m$ is less than some $2^j$, which proves (b). ∎

egmo-2017-06.title: Reflections of the Euler line
egmo-2017-06.body:
We use directed angles $\measuredangle$ modulo $180^\circ$. Let $\Gamma$ be the circumcircle and $H$ the orthocentre. Since the triangle is not equilateral, $G\ne O$, and $O,G,H$ lie on the Euler line $e$. Let $e_1,e_2,e_3$ be the reflections of $e$ in $BC,CA,AB$, and $H_1,H_2,H_3$ the reflections of $H$. Then $O_i,G_i,H_i\in e_i$.

**Fact 1: $H_1,H_2,H_3\in\Gamma$.** Reflection in $BC$ reverses angles, so $\measuredangle BH_1C=-\measuredangle BHC$. Also $\measuredangle BHC=\measuredangle(BH,CH)=\measuredangle(BH,AC)+\measuredangle(AC,AB)+\measuredangle(AB,CH)=90^\circ+\measuredangle CAB+90^\circ=\measuredangle CAB$. Hence $\measuredangle BH_1C=-\measuredangle CAB=\measuredangle BAC$, and $H_1\in\Gamma$. Similarly for $H_2,H_3$. Moreover $H_1\ne H_2$: a common point would lie on the altitudes from $A$ and from $B$, so it would be $H$, which is inside the acute triangle and not on $\Gamma$.

**Fact 2: angles between the reflected lines.** For any line $\ell$, its reflections $\ell_1,\ell_2$ in $BC,CA$ satisfy
$$\measuredangle(\ell_1,\ell_2)=\measuredangle(\ell_1,CB)+\measuredangle(CB,CA)+\measuredangle(CA,\ell_2)=\measuredangle(CB,\ell)+\measuredangle(CB,CA)+\measuredangle(\ell,CA)=2\measuredangle BCA.$$
Applying this to $\ell=CP$ for a point $P\ne C$ with reflections $P_1,P_2$ gives $\measuredangle P_1CP_2=2\measuredangle BCA$. Since the triangle is acute, $2\measuredangle BCA\ne0$. So $e_1\nparallel e_2$, and $C,P_1,P_2$ are not collinear ($CP_1=CP_2$ and the angle $P_1CP_2$ is neither $0^\circ$ nor $180^\circ$). The analogous statements hold at $A$ and $B$.

**Step 1: $e_1,e_2,e_3$ pass through one point $T\in\Gamma$.** Let $T$ be the second intersection of $e_1$ with $\Gamma$ (with $T=H_1$ if $e_1$ is tangent). We show $T\in e_2$.
- If $T=H_2$, this is clear.
- If $T\ne H_1,H_2$: by the inscribed angle theorem and Fact 2, $\measuredangle(e_1,TH_2)=\measuredangle H_1TH_2=\measuredangle H_1CH_2=2\measuredangle BCA=\measuredangle(e_1,e_2)$. So $TH_2$ and $e_2$ are parallel lines through $H_2$, hence equal, and $T\in e_2$.
- If $T=H_1$, then $e_1$ is tangent to $\Gamma$ at $H_1$. By the tangent–chord angle, $\measuredangle(e_1,H_1H_2)=\measuredangle H_1CH_2=\measuredangle(e_1,e_2)$, so again $H_1H_2=e_2$ and $T=H_1\in e_2$.

In the same way (using $B$ and $H_3$), $T\in e_3$. Since $e_1\nparallel e_2$, $T$ is the unique common point of $e_1$ and $e_2$, and likewise of $e_1,e_3$ and of $e_2,e_3$.

**Step 2: $T$ lies on circles $O_1O_2C$ and $G_1G_2C$.** Let $P\in\{O,G\}$, so $P_1\in e_1$ and $P_2\in e_2$, and $C,P_1,P_2$ are not collinear. If $T\in\{P_1,P_2\}$ there is nothing to prove. Otherwise $TP_1=e_1$ and $TP_2=e_2$, so by Fact 2
$$\measuredangle P_1TP_2=\measuredangle(e_1,e_2)=2\measuredangle BCA=\measuredangle P_1CP_2,$$
and $T$ lies on the circle $P_1P_2C$.

In the same way, using the vertices $B$ and $A$ and the pairs $e_1,e_3$ and $e_2,e_3$, $T$ lies on the circles $O_1O_3B$, $G_1G_3B$, $O_2O_3A$, $G_2G_3A$. Together with $T\in\Gamma$, all seven circles pass through $T$. ∎

*Remark.* The proof only used that $O$ and $G$ lie on a line through $H$.
